newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin takes office, Communists ready to join govt.
newsitem.headline: Jospin takes office, Communists ready to join govt.

text.p: Socialist Lionel Jospin took office as France's prime minister on Tuesday following a stunning election win and the Communist party expressed willingness to join his cabinet despite yawning differences over European policy.
Jospin, 59, was expected to name his new cabinet on Wednesday afternoon, a day after taking over as prime minister from conservative Alain Juppe in a brief, stiff ceremony.
Juppe faced a storm of calls to resign from his Gaullist party over its humiliating defeat at the hands of the Socialists and their leftist allies in Sunday's National Assembly election.

Jospin met a succession of senior aides as he tried to put together a cabinet, expected to blend former ministers with new faces in a "Pink-Green-Red" alliance of Socialists, other moderate leftists, Greens and Communists.

The French stock market closed 0.89 percent higher, its third consecutive gain after sharp losses last week. Prices were helped by Socialist assurances that the new government would respect the timetable for a single European currency.

The Communist party, back from the cold and holding the balance of power with 38 seats in the 577-seat Assembly, cleared away a hurdle for Jospin by voicing readiness to take part in the government without setting any clear pre-conditions.

Jospin, who met Communist party boss Robert Hue, has insisted he will not hand policy decisions to anyone outside his Socialist Party. The Socialists broadly favour the euro currency, on certain conditions, while the Communists are opposed.

"The national committee proposes...to reply positively to the question of participation in a leftist parliamentary majority and to that of Communist ministers in the French government," Hue said after a meeting of party bosses.
The party would take a formal decision on Wednesday morning after consulting grassroots members.
The non-Communist left won 274 seats in the election -- short of the 289 needed for a majority.

In the past, the party has said it wants an immediate 500 franc ($86) hike in the monthly minimum wage to 6,906 francs and more vigorous action to cut working hours and create jobs to reduce a record 12.8 percent unemployment rate.
For his handover, a smiling and relaxed Jospin was driven into the courtyard of the Matignon prime ministerial offices, where he shook hands with Juppe, and was ushered inside.

The two men met privately for just 13 minutes before Jospin escorted Juppe back into the courtyard. The outgoing prime minister, wearing a fixed smile, waved cursorily to the crowd, ducked into a waiting car and was driven off at speed.
Out of power, Juppe tried to disarm a barrage of critics within the Rally for the Republic (RPR) by calling a meeting of the party in September to elect a new leader.

"My only concern is the unity of the Gaullist movement," Juppe told reporters. He did not spell out if he would be a candidate for the leadership but made clear he would not stand down immediately to make way for arch-rival Philippe Seguin.
But former interior minister Charles Pasqua and close parliamentary allies of former National Assembly speaker Seguin branded Juppe's timetable unacceptable.
Former prime minister Edouard Balladur met Seguin and said: "I believe very strongly that the RPR should have a movement of renewal...I hope we can find means for unity."
Jospin is likely to make his debut on the world stage on Thursday at a conference of the Socialist International in Malmo, Sweden, aides said.

They said he planned to attend all forthcoming international summits, accompanying conservative President Jacques Chirac with whom he is obliged to "cohabit" during a period of left-right power-sharing.
The move would be a serious attempt to limit the head of state's traditional pre-eminence in the foreign policy realm.
Former prime minister Raymond Barre told the Progres de Lyon daily that Chirac was "in a weakened position" and that he must "now pay the price of failure" without spelling out how.
Jospin has served notice he will not consider implementing further austerity measures, as the previous centre-right government might have done, before the introduction of the euro.
He has argued for a more flexible interpretation of the economic targets for joining monetary union. ($ = 5.825 French Francs)
